newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG chief faces new challenge, army loyalty in doubt.
newsitem.headline: PNG chief faces new challenge, army loyalty in doubt.

text.p: Embattled Papua New Guinea Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan faces a new political challenge to his leadership on Wednesday, as rebel troops blockading the country's parliament refused to pledge loyalty.
About 100 politicians were trapped inside parliament by the rebel soldiers and demonstrators protesting outside after Chan survived a motion on Tuesday to quit.
But leading opposition figure and this impoverished South Pacific nation's first leader, Sir Michael Somare, told a delegation of protest leaders a fresh motion would be moved on Wednesday.
Somare said the protests, which at their height drew about 5,000 demonstrators, could reverse Tuesday's 58-39 losing votes.
"I would like to give you this assurance, that we are going to retry the motion again," Somare told protest leaders outside parliament, under the watchful gaze of heavily armed soldiers.
"At least one thing we can do, we are going to try it again."
Somare later told Reuters the protests may sway some members to switch their support from Chan.
"I think we have a better chance," he said.
The motion is not binding, but Chan's opponents hope a win would shame him into quitting.

Rebel army leader Major Walter Enuma arrived at parliament late on Tuesday night to calm angry troops and reassure the politicians that they were safe and the army would accept parliament's ruling. "We accept the decision of the floor of the parliament and we will allow the normal democratic process to go on, whether it was in favour of what we were fighting for or not," he told Reuters.
Asked if that meant the army would now follow Chan's orders, he said: "The parliament sitting has not been completed yet.
"They will have to sit again and whatever steps they have to take, they will take."
Enuma, who wore a sidearm in his meeting with the politicians, said the parliamentarians should stay for their own safety.
"For their own safety, they should stay in," he said.
Soldiers armed with M-16s and pistols set up road-blocks outside parliament to search cars for any politicians as media, civil servants and diplomats left the building.

Hundreds of anti-government protesters and about 150 soldiers were camped out around the parliament in defiance of the 10 p.m. (1200 GMT) curfew, blocking roads and demanding Chan resign for hiring African mercenaries to end the secessionist conflict on Bougainville island.
Enuma said there would be no trouble from his troops.
"There will be no confrontation. I will not allow it," he said.

Protesters stoned a handful of cars earlier in the day after hearing of the failure of the stand-down motion, and many feared violence would return to the streets of Port Moresby, which was rocked by two days of looting last week.
Parliament voted down a motion urging Chan and two close aides to step pending a probe into the mercenary contract.
Chan himself took the floor only once in the rowdy five-hour debate, saying he had hired the mercenaries to prevent more Papua New Guinea soldiers dying on Bougainville.

"Sometimes you have to make decisions in the best interests of the security of the nation and we made this decision and will not compromise that decision," Chan said. "I had to put the lives of our soldiers on Bougainville first."
The crisis began last Monday when army chief Jerry Singirok demanded the mercenary contract be terminated and that Chan, Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Defence Minister Mathias Ijape resign.

Singirok was promptly sacked but remains in control of the army. His dismissal led to violent street protests that saw former colonial power Australia put troops on standby to evacuate around 10,000 Australian nationals.
Singirok on Friday repeated a demand that Chan quit and set a deadline of Tuesday, but the army remains in its barracks.

About five minutes after Tuesday's vote, ministers were warned to stay inside the building for security reasons as protesters stoned cars leaving parliament. Media cars were also periodically stoned during the evening.
On the other side of the building, around 1,000 noisy protesters were joined by a small group of armed soldiers who sat peacefully on the ground.
The motion against Chan was introduced in parliament by opposition leader Bill Skate, governor of the capital of Port Moresby.

Skate told parliament that the nation was divided and its international credibility was in tatters because Chan agreed to the $36 million contract with British-based mercenary firm Sandline without consulting the cabinet.
"Our nation has been torn apart with division and more and more questions about corruption in high office," Skate told parliament as ministers from both sides shouted each other down.

Defence Minister Ijape said the Sandline contract made financial and military sense. Papua New Guinea spent 120 million Kina ($86 million) a year fighting on Bougainville and had spent a total of 1.2 billion Kina since 1989. Two hundred soldiers had died, as well as 50 policemen and thousands from Bougainville.
Ijape blamed Australia and New Zealand for refusing to supply the Papua New Guinea's defence force with helicopter gunships and other military hardware to fight Bougainville rebels.
